title: A promised dilemma: Rent-to-own home's fate undecided - NewsBreak
text: WARREN, Ohio (WKBN) — Warren City Council heard from Ernestine Charmichael-Owens Wednesday evening, who claims the house she’s been renting on the southwest side should be given to her based on a promise made 25 years ago. The director of the non-profit that owns the home says plans are in the works to sell her the house, but it won’t be free. Ernestine Carmichael-Owens addressed the Warren City Council about her house on Second Street, which in 25 years of renting has cost her $155,000. “I love the home and would like to own the home, which I believe the home has been paid for over three times or more,” Carmichael-Owens said. Council members Helen Rucker and Todd Johnson, along with Mayor Doug Franklin, supported her. “I promise you I’ll use the full weight and power and authority of my office to make sure we get to the bottom of this and find yourself as the homeowner,” Mayor Franklin said. Melissa Phillips is director of Sunshine-Warren Homes, the umbrella agency that owns Charmichael-Owens’ house, and 200 others in Warren where the maximum rent is $750 a month. “I do agree that Ernestine should have the ability to purchase the house,” Phillips said. Phillips says 30 years ago, when the homes were built or renovated, lease-to-own promises were made for people who lived in the houses for 15 years. Those who did were offered the option to buy — but none were sold. Also, there are no contracts. “It seems very likely that would be the case. Grant money might offset that,” Phillips said. “Very likely there will be a cost on the back end.” “I have been a great tenant and believe I should own this home,” Carmichael-Owens said. “We’re going to do all we can to make sure that you have the keys and deed to that property,” Mayor Franklin said. Warren City Council also approved a resolution opposing the Ohio Legislature’s decision to alter the property tax collection process by eliminating the 10 mill inside millage and allowing county budget commissions to determine tax rates. “This bill is detrimental to the financial health of every community,” said councilman Mike O’Brien. “We need to band together from nonsense, to fight together against nonsense,” said Mayor Franklin. “I don’t care what party you are — this hurts everyone.” Council also agreed to place on the November ballot a one-half percent income tax renewal levy. The only difference is previously the levy was for five years. Now council wants to make the tax permanent. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to WYTV.
